title: Sanskrit sounds for readers (the alphabet, in sound)
hook: Krishna in a scholar's book carries a dot under the r, the s and the n, and each dot curls the tongue
carry: let your tongue curl back for it

segments.voice: Yesterday, ka and the map of the mouth: throat, palate, roof, teeth, lips, and c always said ch. The roof was skipped. Today it gets its turn, and the week gets a look back.
screen: `SANSKRIT SOUNDS FOR READERS.` · `THROAT, PALATE, ROOF, TEETH, LIPS.`

segments.voice: Krishna, the way a scholar spells it, has dots hanging under its letters. K. R with a dot. S with a dot. N with a dot. A. Kṛṣṇa. It can look fussy, like footnotes that wandered into the middle of a word. But the dots point to the place skipped yesterday, the roof of the mouth. They tell the tongue to do one thing: curl back.
screen: `KṚṢṆA: A DOT UNDER R, S AND N.` → `NOT FOOTNOTES.` → `THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.`

segments.voice: Put the tip of your tongue behind your top teeth and say ta. That's the teeth row. Now slide the tip back along the roof of your mouth, past the ridge, and curl it up a little. Say ta from there. The sound gets deeper, almost hollow. That's the roof row, and in transliteration its letters get a dot underneath: ṭa, ḍa, ṇa. Linguists call these sounds retroflex: made with the tongue bent back. The same curl gives a second kind of sh. Plain sh, written with an accent on the s, sits at the palate: Śiva. The s with a dot under it is sh with the tongue curled back: Viṣṇu, Kṛṣṇa. And the r with a dot under it is something else again: a vowel. Sanskrit treats a lightly rolled r as a vowel sound in its own right, ṛ. How it's said depends on where you learned it. Some reciters say it close to ri, which is where the English spelling Krishna comes from. Others, in parts of the south and west, say it closer to ru. Both are living ways of saying the same letter. So the name can be read in full: kṛ, with the r-vowel; ṣ, the curled sh; ṇa, the curled n. Now look back at the week. The mudras ended with hands that were received, danced, and found everywhere. Then the sounds began: a, the plainest letter; the line that says stay longer; the map of the mouth; and today, the dot that curls the tongue. Hands, then mouth. Each one a way of letting the body carry meaning.
screen: `THE ROOF ROW: THE TONGUE CURLS BACK.` · `Ś AT THE PALATE, Ṣ CURLED BACK.` · `Ṛ: THE R THAT IS A VOWEL.` · `THE WEEK: HANDS, THEN MOUTH.` · then, large: `THE DOT MEANS: CURL THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Say ta at the teeth, then curl the tongue back and say ṭa at the roof, back and forth a few times; then na and ṇa the same way. Then say the name slowly, piece by piece: kṛ, ṣṇa, Kṛṣṇa. However you've always said it is fine; this is just listening to what the dots ask for, and if you pray, you can let the name be said with care.
Ṛ. The r that is a vowel, alongside the dot underneath that curls the tongue back for ṭ, ḍ, ṇ and ṣ.
Your line: let your tongue curl back for it. Tomorrow, the letters that breathe. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students of Sanskrit practice the retroflex row (ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa) by curling the tongue back to the roof of the mouth, and recite names like Kṛṣṇa and Viṣṇu with these sounds.
